implementation_notes: The portable surface is __builtin_prefetch(addr, rw, locality), supported by GCC and Clang and mapping to the platform's prefetch instruction (prfm on AArch64, prefetcht0/t1/t2/nta on x86). rw is 0 for read and 1 for write; locality is 0 (no temporal locality - evict soon, i.e. non-temporal) through 3 (keep in all levels, the default). For the page-level case, madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) or posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED) does the same job a level down, and readahead() is the older Linux call. There is no C11 prefetch; the intrinsic is the compiler extension that every modern toolchain provides. The x86 mapping is worth internalising because it differs per CPU - NTA, T0 to L1, T1 to L2, T2 to L3 - but the research shows even that is not consistent across vendors.
idiom_name: __builtin_prefetch(addr, rw, locality) plus madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) / posix_fadvise for pages
pitfalls: __builtin_prefetch is a compiler extension, not C11 - it is supported by GCC and Clang but not by every toolchain.
Placing it inside the inner loop inhibits vectorisation; hoist it out or restructure.
The locality level maps to different cache levels per vendor (the research found T2 targeting L1 on AMD and L3 on Grace) - tune on the target.
madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) can return ENOMEM if paging in would exceed RLIMIT_AS, and it is advice: the pages are not guaranteed resident.
